analysis.title: AI meets the neighbours: Are markets pricing AI's social licence to compute?
key_insights: US hyperscaler capex is expected to approach $1tn in 2027, up from about $800bn in 2026e, which was a near-doubling of the 2025 level. The global pipeline of announced data centre capacity for 2025-30 exceeds 100GW, roughly equal to today's installed global capacity.

Data Centre Watch reported at least 75 US data centre projects worth about $130bn were blocked or delayed in Q1 2026, the highest quarterly level since tracking began in 2023. SG puts this at about 18% of the top four hyperscalers' 2026 capex of $725bn.

SG argues the financial risk to data centres' social licence to operate is largely overlooked. Its review of the Sustainalytics universe (about 20,000 companies) found 25 data-centre-related controversies involving 20 companies in 2025-26, all rated Category 1 or 2 (low impact) on a five-point scale.

A low controversy score does not mean low financial risk. Community opposition can lengthen permitting, force project redesign, raise costs and in severe cases delay or prevent development. SG's earlier work shows Social & Community controversies of high severity led to prolonged share-price underperformance.
Of 68 water-related controversies rated Category 3-5, none were directly linked to data centres. Exposure was concentrated in oil and gas, metals and mining, food, forestry and utilities.

Of 85 AI and data centre beneficiaries screened, 35 have lower water and energy intensity than sector peers. YTD to 7 October these returned 70.5%, versus 47.8% for the 50 resource-intensive names and 24.0% for the Nasdaq 100.

Since end-May, when scrutiny of data centre water use intensified, resource-efficient names returned +15.8% versus -3.7% for resource-intensive names and +4.2% for the Nasdaq 100. They beat the intensive group in 15 of 20 weeks and the Nasdaq 100 in 10 of 20. SG says it is too early to establish causality.

The IEA expects data centre electricity use to rise from about 415TWh in 2024 (1.5% of global demand) to about 945TWh by 2030 (about 3%). US consumption is projected to rise 133% from 183TWh to 426TWh.

Studies cited indicate data centre and crypto demand could raise US electricity costs by 6-29% by 2030. Residential electricity prices rose about 25% over 2020-24. Finland removed the preferential electricity-tax rate for data centres from July 2026.

Lower water intensity per unit of compute does not necessarily mean lower total water use while capacity expands quickly. Closed-loop cooling with dry coolers can cut water use a lot, but evaporative systems stay water-intensive. A medium facility uses about 400 million litres a year and hyperscale campuses several billion.

Polling shows 65% of respondents oppose data centre construction in their community (PBS/NPR/Marist), and 58% expect a negative effect on the country. Other surveys put local opposition at 70-75% (Gallup, Heatmap). Data centres are a live issue in the November 2026 US midterms.

Regulation is moving toward a 'cost-causer pays' principle: tighter grid connection and permitting rules, dedicated tariffs, resource-use limits and cost sharing. Examples include Ohio pausing new tax exemptions, New York pausing environmental permits for large hyperscale projects, Denmark's Energinet pausing new large-load grid connections and Utah imposing a stricter statewide framework.
Media coverage linking data centres and water rose 5 times over the past year and 2.5 times since end-May.
SG says investors will likely need to strengthen stewardship on community consultation, infrastructure cost sharing, resource efficiency, site selection and facility-level disclosure.

Seven firms (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, xAI) pledged in March 2026 to supply needed power, fund delivery infrastructure, use separate rates and pay for committed capacity. Google says it will pay for all electricity consumed and growth-driven infrastructure through separate rate structures.

sector_views.rationale: SG sees AI infrastructure investment as structurally strong but flags community opposition as an overlooked cost and timing risk, and favours names with lower water and energy intensity.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Capex growth feeds demand across semiconductors, servers, cloud, connectivity, power and cooling, but is increasingly constrained by power, water and local acceptance.
The load is concentrated in major data centre markets, which could add to grid congestion and electricity costs.
Rising power bills are a central driver of local opposition to data centres.

crypto_views: Studies cited say growing data centre and crypto demand could raise US electricity costs by 6-29% by 2030.

trade_ideas.description: Favour AI and data centre beneficiaries with lower water and energy intensity (35-stock resource-efficient screen) over resource-intensive peers
trade_ideas.rationale: The efficient subset outperformed the intensive group in 15 of 20 weeks since end-May, as water-use scrutiny rose.
trade_ideas.risk: SG says it is too early to establish causality. Past performance is not indicative of future results.

risk_factors: Community opposition lengthens permitting, forces redesign, raises costs and can delay or prevent projects.
Grid strain and higher electricity prices for households and businesses.

Water stress: more than half of India's data centres are in water-stressed areas, and S&P Global estimates 45% of its sample of more than 9,000 data centres could face high water-stress exposure by 2050.
Political and regulatory intervention around the November 2026 US midterms, including pauses on tax exemptions and permits.
Controversy ratings may become more severe if disputes move from protests to operational disruption, which would flow into ESG screening.
Lawsuits alleging procedural violations in project approvals.
geopolitical: Data centres are an issue in the November 2026 US midterm elections, with campaigns at federal and state level.

Europe is tightening planning and grid connection rules. Denmark's Energinet paused new grid connections for large-load projects, and Finland removed the preferential electricity-tax rate for data centres from July 2026.
The Dutch government blocked Meta's Zeewolde project in 2022, and Amsterdam largely prohibited new data centres after a moratorium.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscaler capex is heading toward $1tn in 2027, the announced pipeline exceeds 100GW, and political support for AI infrastructure at the national level remains strong.
tension_points.bear_case: At least 75 US projects worth about $130bn were blocked or delayed in Q1 2026, polls show 65-75% local opposition, and regulators are moving to make large data centres pay more of the power, water and grid costs.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If data centre disputes escalate from protests to operational disruption, controversy ratings would become more severe and more relevant to investor screening.
